title: Almsgiving
lead: Giving to the poor as an act of devotion to God. The law and the prophets command generosity to the poor, the widow, the orphan and the foreigner; books written in the centuries before Jesus, such as Tobit and Sirach, make almsgiving one of the chief marks of a faithful life, and Jesus teaches it with prayer and fasting (Matthew 6:1–18). Churches differ over whether alms help to take away sin.

sections.h: From the law to the Gospels
sections.b: The law tells Israel to open its hand to the poor (Deuteronomy 15:7–11) and to share the third-year tithe with Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows (Deuteronomy 14:28–29). Proverbs says that whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD (Proverbs 19:17), and Daniel urges a king to break off his sins by showing mercy to the oppressed (Daniel 4:27). In later Hebrew the word tsedaqah, "righteousness," came to mean charity, and the Greek translators often used eleēmosynē, "mercy, alms." Jesus tells his followers to give in secret (Matthew 6:2–4), to store up treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:19–21; Luke 12:33), and praises those who fed the hungry and clothed the naked (Matthew 25:35–40). Acts honors Tabitha and Cornelius for their alms (Acts 9:36; Acts 10:2, 4).
